How to use this PDF

  • Clickable contents. The master TOC on the next page — and every cross-reference in this book — is a live link. Click any row, chip, or card ID to jump straight to it.
  • Category color coding. Each of the 13 endorsement categories owns a color (legend below). Category banners, bundle headers, and endorsement cards all wear their category color.
  • Endorsement chips. Inline chips like A.6 jump to that endorsement's full card — verbatim AC text, plain-English notes, and citations.
  • External links. eCFR regulation citations and FAA source links open in your browser and are marked with ↗.
  • PDF bookmarks. Your PDF viewer's outline/bookmark panel mirrors this book's heading structure (parts → categories → bundles → endorsements) for quick navigation.

I certify that [First name, MI, Last name] has received and logged training time within 2 calendar months preceding the month of application in preparation for the practical test and they are prepared for the required practical test for the issuance of [applicable] certificate.

ZZPGM|cat:student-pilot|ZZ

Student Pilot

14 endorsements
ZZPGM|bundle:pre-solo|ZZ

Pre-Solo

Student pilot prerequisites before first solo: TSA eligibility, student pilot certificate, and medical qualification.

Before most airplane students can exercise PIC solo privileges, they need a student pilot certificate, required medical qualification, and the pre-solo training endorsements. Dual instruction may begin before these are fully in place.

Prerequisites before solo

TTSA citizenship / eligibility verification

Flight training providers must handle TSA citizenship or eligibility verification when applicable. If the logbook-endorsement method is used, AC 61-65K A.14 provides commonly used language.

49 CFR § 1552.15(c) AC 61-65K, A.14

IStudent pilot certificate application

Apply through IACRA or an acceptable paper process with an authorized person such as a CFI, DPE, ACR, or FSDO representative. It is not an IACRA-only process.

14 CFR § 61.83 14 CFR § 61.85

MMedical certificate / qualifying medical status

For most private-path airplane students, solo requires at least a third-class medical or another qualifying medical basis that fits the operation being conducted.

14 CFR § 61.3(c) 14 CFR § 61.23

TSA Citizenship / Eligibility

TSA citizenship or eligibility verification is a training-provider compliance item and is separate from the FAA student pilot certificate and separate from medical qualification.

Key Points

  • Training providers must follow applicable TSA citizenship or eligibility verification procedures before providing covered flight training
  • If the provider uses the logbook-endorsement method for U.S. citizenship verification, AC 61-65K A.14 contains commonly used endorsement language
  • This step does not replace the student pilot certificate and does not replace the required medical qualification

Student Pilot Certificate

A student pilot certificate is required before solo flight, but it is not required to begin dual flight instruction.

Eligibility

  • Minimum age 16 for airplane (14 for glider or balloon)
  • Must be able to read, speak, write, and understand English

Application Process

  • Application may be made through IACRA (iacra.faa.gov) or by paper in a form acceptable to the Administrator — 14 CFR 61.85 does not limit the method to IACRA only
  • An authorized person (CFI, DPE, ACR, or FSDO representative) verifies identity and processes or forwards the application as required
  • The FAA does not charge a fee when the certificate is processed through a FSDO; a school, examiner, or other processing entity may charge its own fee

Certificate Issuance & Duration

  • The permanent certificate is mailed; a temporary student pilot certificate may become available in the applicant's IACRA console after processing
  • Student pilot certificates issued after April 1, 2016 no longer expire in the old 24/36-month way — they are generally surrendered when upgrading to a higher certificate
  • Solo endorsements are placed in the logbook, not printed on the student pilot certificate itself

Documents to Carry on Solo Flight

  • Student pilot certificate
  • Photo identification
  • Medical certificate or other qualifying documentation as applicable

Medical Certificate

A separate medical qualification is generally required before solo flight for the normal airplane/private training path. The student pilot certificate and medical qualification are separate requirements and should not be confused.

  • Third-class medical is the typical requirement for most student pilots training toward private or recreational airplane privileges
  • Medical class depends on the privileges being exercised — not simply the highest certificate a pilot may someday hold
  • Commercial privileges generally require at least a second-class medical when those privileges are exercised
  • ATP PIC privileges generally require a first-class medical when those privileges are exercised
  • Some students may qualify under exceptions or different pathways (sport pilot, glider/balloon, certain 61.113(i) operations)

How to Obtain a Medical

  1. Complete the MedXPress application online before your appointment
  2. Schedule an exam with an FAA-designated Aviation Medical Examiner (AME)
  3. Obtain the medical early — do not let it delay solo training

Solo Timeline

  1. Start dual instruction
  2. Apply for the student pilot certificate
  3. Complete TSA citizenship/eligibility verification if applicable
  4. Obtain the required medical qualification
  5. Complete pre-solo aeronautical knowledge test and flight training
  6. Receive the appropriate solo endorsements
  7. Exercise solo privileges only when all required elements are satisfied

Solo privileges may be exercised only when these prerequisites and applicable endorsements are satisfied.

Resources & Regulations

  • IACRA — Integrated Airmen Certification and Rating Application
  • FAA Medical Certification
  • MedXPress — FAA Medical Application
  • Find an Aviation Medical Examiner (AME)

First Solo Featured bundle

Initial daytime solo package for a student pilot.

Primary endorsements

A.3

Pre-solo aeronautical knowledge

Standard CFI signoff No expiration
14 CFR § 61.87(b)
AC 61-65K verbatim · AC page A-7

I certify that [First name, MI, Last name] has satisfactorily completed the pre-solo knowledge test of 14 CFR § 61.87(b) for the [make and model (M/M)] aircraft.

  • Proves the student understands the aircraft, rules, and local procedures before flying alone.
  • Helps confirm the student knows emergency actions and operating limits.
  • Prevents a first solo from happening before the student has the needed knowledge base.
solo student pilot

Pre-solo flight training

Standard CFI signoff No expiration
14 CFR § 61.87(c)(1) and (2)
AC 61-65K verbatim · AC page A-8

I certify that [First name, MI, Last name] has received and logged pre-solo flight training for the maneuvers and procedures that are appropriate to the [M/M] aircraft. I have determined they have demonstrated satisfactory proficiency and safety on the maneuvers and procedures required by 14 CFR § 61.87 in this or similar make and model of aircraft to be flown.

  • Shows the student can safely control the airplane without the instructor onboard.
  • Confirms the student can handle takeoffs, landings, go-arounds, and pattern work.
  • Gives the instructor a documented basis for allowing solo flight.

A.6

Solo flight (first 90-calendar-day period)

Standard CFI signoff 90 calendar days
14 CFR § 61.87(n)
AC 61-65K verbatim · AC page A-8

I certify that [First name, MI, Last name] has received the required training to qualify for solo flying. I have determined they meet the applicable requirements of 14 CFR § 61.87(n) and are proficient to make solo flights in [M/M].

  • This is the student’s main legal authority for first solo flight.
  • Limits the solo to the specific make and model the student was trained in.
  • The 90-day limit forces regular instructor oversight.

Also include if you are using the TSA citizenship logbook endorsement method.

A.14

Endorsement of U.S. citizenship recommended by the Transportation Security Administration (TSA)

Standard CFI signoff No expiration
Title 49 of the Code of Federal Regulations (49 CFR) § 1552.15(c)
AC 61-65K verbatim · AC page A-9

The flight instructor must keep a copy of the documents used to provide proof of citizenship for 5 years or make the following endorsement in the student’s logbook and the instructor’s logbook or other record used to record flight student endorsements with the following: I certify that [First name, MI, Last name] has presented me a [type of document presented, such as a U.S. birth certificate or U.S. passport, and the relevant control or sequential number on the document, if any] establishing that they are a U.S. citizen or national in accordance with 49 CFR § 1552.7(a).

  • Documents that citizenship verification was completed when using the endorsement method.
  • Helps the instructor show compliance with TSA flight training security requirements.
  • Protects both instructor and student if records are later reviewed.
student pilot

ZZPGM|bundle:night-solo|ZZ

Night Solo

Night solo training and authorization endorsement.

Primary endorsements

A.5

Pre-solo flight training at night

Standard CFI signoff 90 calendar days
14 CFR § 61.87(o)
AC 61-65K verbatim · AC page A-8

Flight training must be received within the 90-calendar-day period preceding the date of the flight. I certify that [First name, MI, Last name] has received flight training at night on night flying procedures that include takeoffs, approaches, landings, and go-arounds at night at the [airport name] airport where the solo flight will be conducted; navigation training at night in the vicinity of the [airport name] airport where the solo flight will be conducted. This endorsement expires 90 calendar days from the date the flight training at night was received.

  • Night flying is harder because of reduced visual cues and common illusions.
  • Helps ensure the student knows runway lighting, night procedures, and night judgment.
  • The 90-day limit keeps that night training recent.
solo student pilot

Part II — Workflow Flows

This part walks through the most common real-world sign-off workflows a CFI performs — from a student pilot's pre-solo prerequisites and first solo to checkride packages, flight reviews, and aircraft endorsements. Each numbered step names the exact AC 61-65K endorsement used at that point and links straight to its full card in Part I, so you can jump from the workflow to the verbatim endorsement language and back. Supplemental endorsements that are commonly signed in the same sitting are listed under "Also commonly included."

  • Pre-Solo Student Pilot
  • First Solo Student Pilot
  • Initial Solo XC Student Pilot
  • ASEL Initial Checkride Bundle Private Pilot
  • ASEL Initial Checkride Bundle Commercial Pilot
  • Instrument Checkride Bundle Instrument Rating
  • CFI ASEL Initial Checkride Bundle Flight Instructor
  • Flight Review and WINGS Additional / Recurrent
  • Complex / High-Performance / High-Altitude / Tailwheel Additional / Recurrent
ZZPGM|wf:pre-solo|ZZ

Pre-Solo

Student Pilot

Student pilot prerequisites before first solo: TSA eligibility, student pilot certificate, and medical qualification.

Before most airplane students can exercise PIC solo privileges, they need a student pilot certificate, required medical qualification, and the pre-solo training endorsements. Dual instruction may begin before these are fully in place.

Before the first solo — T · I · M

T TSA citizenship / eligibility verification

Flight training providers must handle TSA citizenship or eligibility verification when applicable. If the logbook-endorsement method is used, AC 61-65K A.14 provides commonly used language.

49 CFR § 1552.15(c) AC 61-65K, A.14
I Student pilot certificate application

Apply through IACRA or an acceptable paper process with an authorized person such as a CFI, DPE, ACR, or FSDO representative. It is not an IACRA-only process.

14 CFR § 61.83 14 CFR § 61.85
M Medical certificate / qualifying medical status

For most private-path airplane students, solo requires at least a third-class medical or another qualifying medical basis that fits the operation being conducted.

14 CFR § 61.3(c) 14 CFR § 61.23

TSA Citizenship / Eligibility

TSA citizenship or eligibility verification is a training-provider compliance item and is separate from the FAA student pilot certificate and separate from medical qualification.

Key Points

  • Training providers must follow applicable TSA citizenship or eligibility verification procedures before providing covered flight training
  • If the provider uses the logbook-endorsement method for U.S. citizenship verification, AC 61-65K A.14 contains commonly used endorsement language
  • This step does not replace the student pilot certificate and does not replace the required medical qualification

Student Pilot Certificate

A student pilot certificate is required before solo flight, but it is not required to begin dual flight instruction.

Eligibility

  • Minimum age 16 for airplane (14 for glider or balloon)
  • Must be able to read, speak, write, and understand English

Application Process

  • Application may be made through IACRA (iacra.faa.gov) or by paper in a form acceptable to the Administrator — 14 CFR 61.85 does not limit the method to IACRA only
  • An authorized person (CFI, DPE, ACR, or FSDO representative) verifies identity and processes or forwards the application as required
  • The FAA does not charge a fee when the certificate is processed through a FSDO; a school, examiner, or other processing entity may charge its own fee

Certificate Issuance & Duration

  • The permanent certificate is mailed; a temporary student pilot certificate may become available in the applicant's IACRA console after processing
  • Student pilot certificates issued after April 1, 2016 no longer expire in the old 24/36-month way — they are generally surrendered when upgrading to a higher certificate
  • Solo endorsements are placed in the logbook, not printed on the student pilot certificate itself

Documents to Carry on Solo Flight

  • Student pilot certificate
  • Photo identification
  • Medical certificate or other qualifying documentation as applicable

Medical Certificate

A separate medical qualification is generally required before solo flight for the normal airplane/private training path. The student pilot certificate and medical qualification are separate requirements and should not be confused.

  • Third-class medical is the typical requirement for most student pilots training toward private or recreational airplane privileges
  • Medical class depends on the privileges being exercised — not simply the highest certificate a pilot may someday hold
  • Commercial privileges generally require at least a second-class medical when those privileges are exercised
  • ATP PIC privileges generally require a first-class medical when those privileges are exercised
  • Some students may qualify under exceptions or different pathways (sport pilot, glider/balloon, certain 61.113(i) operations)

How to Obtain a Medical

  1. Complete the MedXPress application online before your appointment
  2. Schedule an exam with an FAA-designated Aviation Medical Examiner (AME)
  3. Obtain the medical early — do not let it delay solo training

Solo Timeline

  1. Start dual instruction
  2. Apply for the student pilot certificate
  3. Complete TSA citizenship/eligibility verification if applicable
  4. Obtain the required medical qualification
  5. Complete pre-solo aeronautical knowledge test and flight training
  6. Receive the appropriate solo endorsements
  7. Exercise solo privileges only when all required elements are satisfied

Solo privileges may be exercised only when these prerequisites and applicable endorsements are satisfied.

Part III — Guidance

Part I cataloged what each endorsement says. This part turns that catalog into operational guidance: the student journey from enrollment to checkride shows when each endorsement is used, and the DPE scenarios walk through the situations where the paperwork most often goes wrong.

In this part Student Journey DPE Scenarios
ZZPGM|gs:journey|ZZ

Student Journey

The 12 stages of a student's training, grouped by phase — from enrollment through the checkride — with the regulation, endorsements, time limits, and gotchas that apply at each step. Endorsement chips jump to the full card in Part I.

Pre-Solo3 stages

1Enrollment

Before training begins, the student needs a student pilot certificate, qualifying medical, and TSA citizenship/eligibility verification. Dual instruction may start before these are fully in place.

Regulation 14 CFR § 61.83 14 CFR § 61.85 14 CFR § 61.23 49 CFR § 1552.15(c)
Gotchas
  • TSA verification is a training-provider compliance item — separate from the student pilot certificate and medical
  • Student pilot certificates no longer expire (rule change) — but medical and endorsements still do
  • IACRA or paper process accepted; CFI, DPE, ACR, or FSDO rep may act as authorized person
Notes
  • TSA Citizenship A.14 — If using the logbook-endorsement method for U.S. citizenship, AC 61-65K A.14 provides the language

2Pre-Solo Ground

Before the first solo, the student must pass a knowledge test on all 14 subject areas in FAR 61.87(b) (A.3) and receive flight training in the maneuvers and procedures of FAR 61.87(c) (A.4). Both endorsements must be in the logbook before solo.

Regulation 14 CFR § 61.87(b) 14 CFR § 61.87(c)(1)&(2)
Endorsements A.3 Pre-solo aeronautical knowledge A.4 Pre-solo flight training
Gotchas
  • All 14 knowledge areas in 61.87(b) must be covered — not a subset
  • A.3 (ground) and A.4 (flight) are two separate endorsements — both required before solo
  • Must be given by an authorized instructor
  • The instructor who gives the flight training must also sign the A.6 solo endorsement

3Pre-Solo Night (if applicable)

If the student will fly solo at night, the instructor must give specific night flight training at the airport where the solo will occur. The A.5 endorsement expires 90 calendar days from when the night training was received.

Regulation 14 CFR § 61.87(o)
Time limit90 calendar days from date of night training
Endorsements A.5 Pre-solo flight training at night
Gotchas
  • A.5 is only required if the student will solo at night — not required for daytime solo
  • Training must be at the specific airport where night solo will occur
  • A.5 expires 90 days from the training date — not the endorsement date
  • A.5 is in addition to A.3 and A.4, not a replacement for either

Solo3 stages

4First Solo

Before the student's first solo, all three endorsements must be in the logbook: A.3 (pre-solo knowledge test), A.4 (pre-solo flight training), and A.6 (solo authorization for a specific make and model). The A.6 opens a 90-day solo window and may only be issued by the instructor who gave the training.

Regulation 14 CFR § 61.87(b) 14 CFR § 61.87(c)(1)&(2) 14 CFR § 61.87(n)
Time limit90 calendar days from date of A.6 endorsement
Endorsements A.3 Pre-solo aeronautical knowledge A.4 Pre-solo flight training A.6 Solo flight (first 90-calendar-day period)
Gotchas
  • All three endorsements — A.3, A.4, and A.6 — must be in the logbook before first solo
  • Specific make AND model must be in A.6 — not just 'Cessna' but 'Cessna 172S'
  • Only the instructor who provided the training may issue the A.6 (first solo)
  • After 90 days, the student cannot act as PIC without a new A.7 endorsement
  • The 90-day clock starts on the date of the A.6 endorsement, not the date of first flight

5Solo Renewal

Each time the 90-day solo window expires, an authorized instructor must review the student and issue a new A.7 endorsement to authorize another 90-day period. Unlike A.6, any authorized CFI may issue A.7 renewals.

Regulation 14 CFR § 61.87(p)
Time limit90 calendar days from date of endorsement
Endorsements A.7 Solo flight (each additional 90-calendar-day period)
Gotchas
  • Any authorized CFI may issue A.7 renewals — doesn't have to be the original instructor
  • The instructor must actually review the student before endorsing — not a rubber stamp
  • Each renewal opens a new 90-day window — not an extension of the original
  • Student cannot fly solo PIC after the A.6 (or previous A.7) expires, even briefly

6Local Solo Ops

To fly to another specific airport within 25 NM, the student needs an A.8 endorsement naming that airport. This is separate from the cross-country authorization.

Regulation 14 CFR § 61.93(b)(1)
Endorsements A.8 Solo takeoffs and landings at another airport within 25 NM
Gotchas
  • Each airport must be specifically named in the endorsement
  • 25 NM radius from the originating airport
  • This is NOT the same as a cross-country endorsement

Cross-Country4 stages

7XC Training

Two endorsements are required for solo cross-country flights. A.9 is the one-time category authorization confirming the student received XC training. A.10 must be issued before each individual solo XC flight after reviewing the specific flight plan, weather, and route.

Regulation 14 CFR § 61.93(c)(1)&(2) 14 CFR § 61.93(c)(3)
Endorsements A.9 Solo cross-country flight (category authorization) A.10 Solo cross-country flight (per-flight planning review)
Gotchas
  • A.9 is the general XC training authorization — it does not approve any specific flight
  • A.10 is required before EVERY individual solo XC flight — no blanket authorization
  • A.10 review must occur before each flight — must check weather, NOTAMs, route, fuel
  • Category-specific — A.9 covers airplanes; different category would need a new endorsement
  • A.11 may replace per-flight A.10 for repeated short-range XC routes (within 50 NM)

8XC Per-Flight

Before each solo cross-country flight, the student must present their flight plan to an authorized instructor, who reviews it and endorses the student's logbook for that specific flight.

Regulation 14 CFR § 61.93(c)(3)
Endorsements A.10 Solo cross-country flight planning (per individual flight)
Gotchas
  • A.10 is required before EVERY individual solo XC flight — no blanket authorization
  • Must review weather, NOTAMs, route, alternates, fuel — the whole plan
  • The review must occur before each flight, not at the beginning of the week
  • Exception: A.11 may replace per-flight endorsements for repeated short-range XC flights

9Repeated Short XC

For repeated solo flights to the same destination within 50 NM (e.g., a practice XC route), an instructor may issue a single A.11 endorsement covering multiple flights rather than requiring A.10 before each one.

Regulation 14 CFR § 61.93(b)(2)
Endorsements A.11 Repeated solo cross-country flights not more than 50 NM
Gotchas
  • Route must not exceed 50 NM from departure airport
  • This replaces the per-flight A.10 only for these specific repeated flights
  • Still requires A.9 general XC authorization

10Class B (if req.)

If the student's training requires flight in or to a Class B airport, specific endorsements are required. A.12 covers general Class B airspace; A.13 covers the specific Class B airport.

Regulation 14 CFR § 61.95(a) 14 CFR § 61.95(b) 14 CFR § 91.131(b)(1)
Endorsements A.12 Solo flight in Class B airspace A.13 Solo flight to/from/at a Class B airport
Gotchas
  • Not all students need this — only required if their training involves Class B airspace
  • A.12 (airspace) and A.13 (airport) are two distinct endorsements
  • The DPE will ask about these even if not applicable to your students — know the requirement

Checkride2 stages

11Knowledge Test

Before sitting for the FAA written knowledge test, the applicant must be endorsed by an authorized instructor certifying they received the required ground training or completed a home-study course. For private pilot airplane: A.36. The specific endorsement number varies by certificate level.

Regulation 14 CFR § 61.35(a)(1) 14 CFR § 61.103(d) 14 CFR § 61.105
Endorsements A.36 Aeronautical knowledge test — Private Pilot (ASEL)
Gotchas
  • A.36 is the Private Pilot example — commercial (A.38), instrument (A.42), CFI (A.46) each have their own endorsement
  • A knowledge test result is valid for 24 calendar months for use at a practical test
  • The endorsement must be in the logbook before the applicant sits for the written test
  • A separate A.2 endorsement is required after the test to address any missed areas

12Checkride Bundle

The complete private pilot checkride endorsement package (ASEL example) requires four endorsements: A.36 (knowledge test prep, issued before the written), A.2 (knowledge test deficiency review, issued after the written), A.37 (flight proficiency, issued before the practical test), and A.1 (prerequisites, issued within 2 calendar months of the practical test).

Regulation 14 CFR § 61.39(a)(6)
Time limitA.1 must be issued within 2 calendar months preceding the month of application
Endorsements A.36 Aeronautical knowledge test — Private Pilot (ASEL) A.2 Review of deficiencies identified on airman knowledge test A.37 Flight proficiency / practical test — Private Pilot (ASEL) A.1 Prerequisites for practical test
Gotchas
  • A.36 comes first — must be in logbook before the applicant sits for the knowledge test
  • A.2 must be issued AFTER the knowledge test report is received, and BEFORE the checkride
  • A.37 (PPL) confirms flight proficiency — this is the certificate-specific endorsement
  • A.1 is the 'prerequisites' endorsement — it expires if not used within 2 calendar months
  • Every practical test attempt — pass or fail — uses up the A.1; a new one is required for any retest
  • IACRA is preferred; most DPEs now require it. Paper 8710-1 is still accepted
  • Applicant must hold at least a current third-class medical (FAR 61.23) in most cases
ZZPGM|gs:scenarios|ZZ

DPE Scenarios

8 real-world situations examiners and instructors actually face, walked through step by step — with the endorsements each one triggers and the deadlines and pitfalls to watch. Endorsement chips jump to the full card in Part I.

Student failed one or more areas of operation on the checkrideRetesting

Regulation 14 CFR § 61.43(f) 14 CFR § 61.49
  1. The practical test is complete — the attempt uses up the A.1 endorsement regardless of outcome
  2. The DPE issues a Notice of Disapproval (or unsatisfactory area notation if partial)
  3. The student must receive additional training in the failed area(s)
  4. The instructor must issue a new A.77 endorsement (retesting after failure) confirming training was given
  5. A new A.1 (prerequisites) endorsement is also required — within 2 calendar months of the new application
  6. Re-submit IACRA (or new 8710-1) before the retest
  7. If the retest is for specific failed areas only, it must be completed within 60 calendar days of the original test date to retain credit for passed areas
Endorsements A.77 Retesting after failure of a knowledge or practical test A.1 Prerequisites for practical test (new endorsement required)
Time limit60 calendar days from the original test date to complete remainder and retain credit for passed areas
Pitfalls
  • Students often don't realize a new A.1 AND A.77 are both required — not just A.77
  • The 60-day clock runs from the original test date, not the date of disapproval paperwork
  • After 60 calendar days, ALL areas must be re-tested from scratch

DPE issued a Letter of Discontinuance (weather, aircraft, safety of flight)Retesting

Regulation 14 CFR § 61.43(e)-(f)
  1. The DPE issues a Letter of Discontinuance — this is NOT a failure
  2. The applicant retains credit for areas of operation already passed
  3. No new A.77 endorsement is required (discontinuance is not a failure)
  4. The existing A.1 must still be valid (within 2 calendar months) for the continuation
  5. The remainder of the test must be completed within 60 calendar days of the original start date
  6. The same DPE is not required for the continuation — any qualified DPE may complete it
Time limit60 calendar days from the original test date to complete the remainder
Pitfalls
  • After 60 calendar days, all areas must be re-tested — the Letter of Discontinuance credit expires
  • If the A.1 endorsement also expires (2-month limit), a new one must be issued before continuing
  • Discontinuance ≠ Failure — no A.77 needed, no new A.1 unless the 2-month window expired

Pilot wants to add a multiengine class rating to existing single-engine private certificateAdditional Ratings

Regulation 14 CFR § 61.63(c)
  1. Adding a class rating within the same category — FAR 61.63(c) applies
  2. No knowledge test required (applicant already holds private certificate at the same level)
  3. No need to meet the flight-time requirements for an initial class rating
  4. Provide required flight training in the multiengine airplane
  5. Issue A.78 (additional aircraft category/class rating) and A.1 (practical test prerequisites)
  6. If the multiengine airplane is complex, also issue A.72 (complex aircraft endorsement)
  7. Complete IACRA or 8710-1 and schedule the practical test
Endorsements A.1 Prerequisites for practical test A.78 Additional aircraft category or class rating (other than ATP) A.72 To act as PIC in a complex aircraft (if applicable)
Time limitA.1 must be within 2 calendar months preceding the month of application
Pitfalls
  • Forgetting A.72 if the multiengine training aircraft is also complex (retractable gear + controllable prop + flaps)
  • No knowledge test ≠ no preparation — the oral still covers all applicable ACS areas
  • CFII required if adding instrument privileges concurrently

60 calendar days have passed since the Letter of Discontinuance or partial failureTime Limits

Regulation 14 CFR § 61.43(f)(1)
  1. Once 60 calendar days pass from the original test date, all credit for passed areas of operation is lost
  2. The applicant must re-accomplish the entire practical test
  3. A new A.1 endorsement is required (within 2 calendar months of the new application)
  4. If the original test ended in failure, a new A.77 is also required after additional training
  5. Re-submit IACRA or 8710-1 before the new attempt
Endorsements A.1 Prerequisites for practical test (new endorsement) A.77 Retesting after failure (if original was a failure, not discontinuance)
Pitfalls
  • The 60-day window closes at midnight on the 60th calendar day — not 60 business days
  • Even if the student passed 9 of 10 areas, after 60 days everything resets
  • The 60-day limit and the 2-calendar-month A.1 expiration are separate — both must be checked

Pilot needs a biennial flight review (BFR)Recurrent

Regulation 14 CFR § 61.56(a)&(c)
  1. Any authorized CFI may conduct a flight review — instrument rating or additional ratings not required
  2. Minimum: 1 hour of flight training + 1 hour of ground training
  3. Ground must include review of 14 CFR Part 91 rules and regs
  4. Flight must include maneuvers and procedures that the instructor deems necessary
  5. If satisfactorily completed: endorse the pilot's logbook with A.69
  6. If not completed satisfactorily: no entry noting unsatisfactory performance is required; however, log the instruction given in your records
Endorsements A.69 Flight review completion
Time limitRequired within the preceding 24 calendar months (per FAR 61.56)
Pitfalls
  • No logbook entry for 'failed flight review' is required — and making one could be harmful to the pilot
  • The instructor must still log the instruction given in their own records (FAR 61.189)
  • A practical test or proficiency check for any certificate/rating also satisfies the flight review requirement

Instrument-rated pilot needs an Instrument Proficiency Check (IPC)Recurrent

Regulation 14 CFR § 61.57(d)
  1. An IPC requires a CFII (Certificated Flight Instructor – Instrument) — a standard CFI cannot conduct one
  2. May be conducted in aircraft or an approved FTD/ATD
  3. Must include the tasks and maneuvers in the Instrument Rating ACS or the instrument section of the applicable PTS
  4. If satisfactorily completed: endorse the pilot's logbook with A.71
  5. If not completed: no unsatisfactory-performance entry required; log instruction given in your records
Endorsements A.71 Instrument proficiency check completion
Time limitRequired when instrument currency (6 approaches, holds, tracking, interception in preceding 6 calendar months) has lapsed
Pitfalls
  • A standard CFI (not CFII) cannot conduct an IPC
  • An IPC is different from instrument currency — currency is self-conducted; an IPC resets it after a lapse
  • No unsatisfactory-performance entry required — same rule as the flight review

Student or pilot wants to solo an aircraft in a category/class they don't holdSpecial

Regulation 14 CFR § 61.31(d)(2)
  1. FAR 61.31(d)(2) allows solo flight without the appropriate category/class rating if training has been received
  2. The instructor must have given the required training for that category/class
  3. Issue A.76 endorsement (Solo PIC when pilot does not hold appropriate category/class rating)
  4. Log the endorsement in the student's logbook and in your instructor records
Endorsements A.76 Solo PIC when pilot does not hold appropriate category/class
Pitfalls
  • A.76 does not grant a rating — it is a limited endorsement allowing solo for training purposes only
  • The instructor must be authorized to give training in that category/class
  • This also applies to students training for an additional rating (e.g., helicopter, glider, multiengine)

Practical test was planned in increments and not completed on the same dateTime Limits

Regulation 14 CFR § 61.39(g)-(h)
  1. Some examiners conduct practical tests in planned increments (e.g., oral one day, flight another day)
  2. FAR 61.39(g) requires all increments to be completed within 2 calendar months of the date the first increment was completed
  3. If not completed within 2 calendar months, the entire test must be re-accomplished (FAR 61.39(h))
  4. A new A.1 endorsement is required before any re-accomplishment
Endorsements A.1 Prerequisites for practical test (new endorsement if re-accomplishing)
Time limit2 calendar months from the date the first increment was completed
Pitfalls
  • This 2-month limit is SEPARATE from the 60-day discontinuance credit window
  • The 2-month limit applies even if there was no failure or discontinuance — it applies to planned multi-day tests
  • '2 calendar months' means through the last day of the month that is 2 months later — e.g., test started March 15 → must complete by May 31

CFI Career — Renewal, Reinstatement & Trainer Qualification

Everything about keeping the instructor certificate itself alive: the December 2024 rule change, the six renewal pathways, reinstatement after expiration, and who may train initial CFI applicants.

Renewal Rules — Before vs. After December 1, 2024

Issued Before December 1, 2024

Certificates issued before December 1, 2024 expire 24 calendar months from the month issued, renewed, or reinstated (Exception: FAR 61.197(b)). Renewal is required every 2 years.

Issued On or After December 1, 2024

Certificates issued on or after December 1, 2024 are issued without an expiration date. However, instructors must still satisfy recent experience requirements every 24 calendar months to maintain instructional privileges.

Renewal Pathways

PathwayTime FrameDescriptionNotes
Pass a Practical Test Within previous 24 calendar months Pass a practical test for one of the ratings listed on your instructor certificate, or for an additional flight instructor rating. Most direct path — also adds or upgrades your ratings.
80% Pass Rate — 5+ Applicants Within previous 24 calendar months Submit documentation showing you endorsed 5 or more applicants for a practical test and achieved an 80% or better first-attempt pass rate. Qualifying for a Gold Seal certificate may be done simultaneously.
Evaluative Position Within previous 24 calendar months Serve in an evaluative or instructional oversight role: company check pilot, check airman, chief flight instructor, Part 121 or 135 instructor, or similar qualified position. Must hold the position and conduct evaluations during that 24-month window.
Approved FIRC Within previous 3 calendar months Complete a Flight Instructor Refresher Course (FIRC) that meets the standards of AC 61-83. Shorter window than other pathways — 3 months, not 24. Plan accordingly.
Military Proficiency Check Within previous 24 calendar months Pass a military instructor pilot or pilot examiner proficiency check in an aircraft within the preceding 24 calendar months. Applies to military instructor pilots maintaining both FAA and military credentials.
FAA WINGS Program 1 Phase completed within previous 12 months; 15 activities evaluated Complete an FAA-sponsored pilot proficiency program (WINGS) meeting all three conditions: hold a current CFI, complete at least 1 phase in the last 12 months, and evaluate and endorse 15 flight activities for at least 5 different pilots. See AC 61-91 for full WINGS program details. All three conditions must be met simultaneously.

Reinstatement After Expiration

Expired ≤ 3 Calendar Months

An expired certificate may be reinstated via an approved FIRC (Flight Instructor Refresher Course) that meets AC 61-83 standards.

No instructional privileges may be exercised during this reinstatement period — until the application is submitted and the certificate is reinstated.

Expired > 3 Calendar Months

Must pass a practical test for one of the ratings on the expired certificate, a practical test for an additional flight instructor rating, or a military instructor pilot/pilot examiner proficiency check.

A FIRC alone is not sufficient after the 3-month window closes. A full practical test is required.

Submit an Airman Certificate and/or Rating Application (Form 8710-1 or 8710-11) to validate recent experience or reinstate privileges.

Qualifying to Train Initial CFI Applicants

Effective December 1, 2024

Ground training options

  • Held the appropriate instructor certificate for 24+ months AND given 40+ hours of ground training, OR
  • Held the appropriate instructor certificate AND given 100+ hours of ground training in an FAA-approved course

Flight training options

  • Held a flight instructor certificate for at least 24 months AND given at least 200 hours of flight training, OR
  • Maintained an 80%+ practical test pass rate for at least 5 applicants in the last 24 months, OR
  • Provided 200 hours of flight training AND completed a Flight Instructor Enhanced Qualification Training Program (FIEQTP) under Part 141 — per FAR 61.95(h)(3) and AC 61-145

DPE Prep Flashcards

Fifteen oral-exam-style questions covering the endorsement knowledge DPEs actually probe. Answers link back to the full endorsement cards and the governing regulations.

Student Endorsements 1 / 15

Q: What are the three pre-solo endorsements a student must have before their first solo flight?

A.3 — Pre-solo aeronautical knowledge (FAR 61.87(b)), A.4 — Pre-solo flight training (FAR 61.87(c)), and A.5 — Pre-solo flight training at night (FAR 61.87(o)) if night solo is planned. All must be in the logbook before the first solo.

Student Endorsements 2 / 15

Q: How long is a first solo endorsement (A.6) valid, and who may issue it?

90 calendar days from the date of the endorsement (FAR 61.87(n)). The instructor who gave the training must issue the A.6 first solo endorsement. The endorsement must list the specific make and model of aircraft.

Student Endorsements 3 / 15

Q: Your student's 90-day solo endorsement expired yesterday. What must you do before they fly solo again?

Review the student and issue a new A.7 endorsement (solo flight — each additional 90-day period, FAR 61.87(p)). Any authorized CFI may issue A.7 renewals — it does not have to be the original instructor.

Student Endorsements 4 / 15

Q: What endorsement is required before each individual solo cross-country flight, and what must the instructor review?

A.10 — Solo cross-country flight planning (FAR 61.93(c)(3)). Before each flight, the instructor must review: the route, weather, NOTAMs, fuel requirements, and alternates. It cannot be issued in advance for future flights.

Logbook Entries 5 / 15

Q: What are the 8 required elements of a logbook entry under FAR 61.51?

(1) Date, (2) Aircraft identification (N-number), (3) Aircraft make and model, (4) Type of experience (Solo, PIC, Dual, etc.), (5) Total flight time, (6) Flight conditions (Day, Night, Instrument, Simulated Instrument), (7) Departure and arrival locations, (8) Name of safety pilot, if required.

Logbook Entries 6 / 15

Q: How long must a CFI retain records of endorsements, and what records are required?

At least 3 years (FAR 61.189). Required records: (1) name of each person endorsed for solo flight and the date of endorsement, (2) name of each person endorsed for a knowledge or practical test, the kind of test, date, and results.

Practical Test 7 / 15

Q: Within what time frame must the A.1 (prerequisites for practical test) endorsement be issued?

Within 2 calendar months preceding the month of application (FAR 61.39(a)(6)). For example, if the checkride is in May, the A.1 must have been issued in March, April, or May.

Practical Test 8 / 15

Q: Your student fails the knowledge test. What must you do before they can take the practical test?

Review all areas of deficiency identified on the Airman Knowledge Test Report, then issue an A.2 endorsement (review of deficiencies, FAR 61.39(a)(6)(iii)) confirming the student now has satisfactory knowledge in those areas. The A.2 is required before every practical test.

Retesting 9 / 15

Q: Your student fails one area of operation on the checkride. What endorsements are needed before the retest, and what time limit applies?

Both A.77 (retesting after failure, after additional training, FAR 61.49) AND a new A.1 (prerequisites, within 2 calendar months). To retain credit for passed areas, the remainder must be completed within 60 calendar days of the original test date (FAR 61.43(f)).

Retesting 10 / 15

Q: What is the difference between the 60-calendar-day limit and the 2-calendar-month limit?

60 calendar days (FAR 61.43(f)): governs credit retention for passed areas after discontinuance or partial failure — after 60 days, all areas must be re-tested. 2 calendar months (FAR 61.39(g)): governs completion of a practical test conducted in planned increments — if not done in 2 months, entire test must be re-accomplished. Neither is related to the 90-day solo window.

Recurrent 11 / 15

Q: A pilot's flight review has lapsed. Who can conduct it, what are the minimums, and what endorsement is given?

Any authorized CFI. Minimum: 1 hour of ground training (reviewing Part 91) and 1 hour of flight training. After satisfactory completion: A.69 endorsement in the pilot's logbook (FAR 61.56(a)&(c)). No unsatisfactory-performance entry is required if the review is not completed, but log the instruction given.

Recurrent 12 / 15

Q: Who can conduct an IPC, and what endorsement is given?

Only a CFII (Certificated Flight Instructor – Instrument) — a standard CFI cannot conduct an IPC. After satisfactory completion: A.71 in the pilot's logbook (FAR 61.57(d)). As with the flight review, no unsatisfactory-performance entry is required, but log the instruction.

CFI Career 13 / 15

Q: Name the 6 ways a CFI can satisfy the recent experience requirement to maintain instructional privileges.

(1) Pass a practical test for a rating on the certificate or additional instructor rating. (2) Document 5+ applicants endorsed for checkride with 80%+ first-attempt pass rate. (3) Hold an evaluative position (check pilot, chief instructor, Part 121/135 instructor). (4) Complete an approved FIRC (within 3 calendar months). (5) Pass a military instructor/examiner proficiency check. (6) Complete the FAA WINGS program. All must be within the previous 24 calendar months (FIRC: 3 months).

CFI Career 14 / 15

Q: Your CFI certificate expired 2 months ago. How do you reinstate it?

Within 3 calendar months of expiration: complete an approved FIRC (AC 61-83). No instructional privileges may be exercised during this period — submit the application first. Then reinstatement is processed. You may NOT instruct while expired even if the FIRC is done.

CFI Career 15 / 15

Q: Your CFI certificate expired 5 months ago. What must you do to reinstate it?

After 3 calendar months of expiration, a FIRC alone is insufficient. You must pass a practical test for one of the ratings on your expired certificate, a practical test for an additional instructor rating, or a military instructor pilot/pilot examiner proficiency check (FAR 61.199, effective December 1, 2024).

Lesson Plan — Teaching Endorsements

A ten-part ground lesson for CFI candidates and working instructors on issuing, managing, and verifying AC 61-65K endorsements.

  1. 1. Lesson Objectives & Key Elements
  2. 2. Logbook Entries & Required Records
  3. 3. Student Pilot Certificate Endorsements
  4. 4. Practical Test Preparation & Recommendation
  5. 5. Additional Ratings & Retesting
  6. 6. Time Limits: 60 Calendar Days vs. 2 Calendar Months
  7. 7. Flight Review & Instrument Proficiency Check Endorsements
  8. 8. Flight Instructor Responsibilities
  9. 9. Maintaining Your CFI Certificate & WINGS Program
  10. 10. Conclusion & Verification
ZZPGM|gs:objectives|ZZ

1. Lesson Objectives & Key Elements

References

  • 14 CFR Part 61
  • AC 61-65K – Certification: Pilots and Flight and Ground Instructors
  • AC 61-98 – Currency Requirements and Guidance for the Flight Review and Instrument Proficiency Check
  • AC 61-83 – Flight Instructor Refresher Course
  • AC 61-91 – WINGS Pilot Proficiency Program
  • FAA Order 8900.1 (FSIMS)

Objective

The learner should develop knowledge of the elements related to logbook entries and endorsements as required by the appropriate Airman Certification Standards (ACS).

Key Elements

  1. AC 61-65
  2. Endorsements
  3. Required Records
  4. Logbook Entries
  5. Student Pilot Certificate Endorsements
  6. Preparation of a Practical Test Recommendation
  7. Additional Ratings
  8. Reapplying for a Practical Test
  9. Time Limits
  10. Flight Review Endorsements
  11. Flight Instructor Responsibilities
  12. Maintaining Your CFI Certificate

Lesson Schedule

  1. Discuss objectives
  2. Review material
  3. Development
  4. Conclusion

Instructor & Student Actions

  • Instructor: Discuss lesson objectives, present lecture, ask and answer questions, assign homework
  • Student: Participate in discussion, take notes, ask and respond to questions

Completion Standards

The learner understands what is necessary in their logbooks, what is required for student pilot certificates and preparing a learner for a practical test, and the requirements for flight review endorsements and flight instructor records.

ZZPGM|gs:logbook|ZZ

2. Logbook Entries & Required Records

Instructor Logbook Signing Requirement (FAR 61.51)

A flight instructor must sign the logbook of each person to whom they have given flight or ground training. Required elements of a logbook entry under FAR 61.51:

  • Date
  • Aircraft identification
  • Aircraft make and model
  • Type of experience (Solo, PIC, etc.)
  • Total flight time
  • Flight conditions (Day, Night, Instrument, etc.)
  • Location of departure and arrival
  • Name of safety pilot, if required

Recordkeeping Requirements (FAR 61.189)

An instructor must maintain a record in a logbook or separate document containing:

  • Name of each person endorsed for solo flight privileges, and the date of the endorsement
  • Name of each person endorsed for a knowledge or practical test, with the kind of test, date, and results

These records must be retained for at least 3 years.

Unsatisfactory Performance

No logbook entry reflecting unsatisfactory performance on a flight review or instrument proficiency check is required. However, a logbook entry for the instruction given should still be made.

ZZPGM|gs:student-endorsements|ZZ

3. Student Pilot Certificate Endorsements

Pre-Solo Endorsements

  • Pre-solo aeronautical knowledge – FAR 61.87(b), AC 61-65 A.3
  • Pre-solo flight training – FAR 61.87(c)(1)&(2), AC 61-65 A.4
  • Pre-solo flight training at night – FAR 61.87(o), AC 61-65 A.5

Solo Flight Endorsements

  • Solo flight (first 90-day period) – FAR 61.87(n), AC 61-65 A.6 — endorsement for the specific make & model by the instructor who gave the training within the preceding 90 days
  • Solo flight (each additional 90-day period) – FAR 61.87(p), AC 61-65 A.7
  • Solo takeoffs and landings at another airport within 25 NM – FAR 61.93(b)(1), AC 61-65 A.8

Cross-Country Endorsements

  • Solo cross-country training (category-specific) – FAR 61.93(c)(1)&(2), AC 61-65 A.9
  • Solo cross-country flight planning (make & model-specific) – FAR 61.93(c)(3), AC 61-65 A.10 — required for each individual cross-country flight
  • Repeated solo cross-country flights not more than 50 NM from departure – FAR 61.93(b)(2), AC 61-65 A.11

Class B Airspace Endorsements

  • Solo flight in Class B airspace – FAR 61.95(a), AC 61-65 A.12
  • Solo flight to/from/at a Class B airport – FAR 61.95(b) & FAR 91.131(b)(1), AC 61-65 A.13

TSA U.S. Citizenship Endorsement

The instructor must keep a copy of the documents used to provide proof of citizenship for 5 years, or make the following endorsement:

  • AC 61-65 A.14 – Endorsement of U.S. Citizenship recommended by the TSA: 49 CFR 1552.3(h)

Special Federal Aviation Regulations (SFARs)

SFARs are temporary regulations issued by the FAA that apply to specific people and aircraft, often with an expiration date that can be amended, extended, or rescinded.

  • SFAR 73 – Robinson R-22/R-44 Special Training & Experience Requirements (not applicable to airplanes, but sample endorsements appear in AC 61-65)
  • SFAR 100-2 – Relief for U.S. Military/Civilians assigned outside the U.S. in support of Armed Forces operations
  • Part 91 SFARs generally prohibit flight in specific regions (e.g., Damascus, Somalia, Pyongyang, Tehran)

Review applicable SFARs whenever endorsing a student operating under special regulatory conditions.

ZZPGM|gs:practical-test|ZZ

4. Practical Test Preparation & Recommendation

Prerequisites Endorsement — AC 61-65 A.1

Except as provided by FAR 61.39, each applicant must receive an endorsement from an authorized instructor certifying that the applicant received and logged the required flight time and training in preparation for the practical test within 2 calendar months preceding the month of application, and is prepared for the test.

Knowledge-Test Deficiency Review — AC 61-65 A.2

The instructor must endorse the applicant after reviewing areas of deficiency identified on the Airman Knowledge Test Report. This confirms the applicant has satisfactory knowledge of those subject areas. It is sometimes combined with the A.1 endorsement (e.g., AC 61-65 A.44 for instrument rating).

Example: Single-Engine Private Pilot Endorsements

  1. AC 61-65 A.1 – Prerequisites for a Practical Test: FAR 61.39(a)(6)(i)&(ii)
  2. AC 61-65 A.2 – Review of Deficiencies Identified on Airman Knowledge Test: FAR 61.39(a)(6)(iii)
  3. AC 61-65 A.36 – Aeronautical Knowledge Test: FAR 61.35(a)(1), 61.103(d), 61.105
  4. AC 61-65 A.37 – Flight Proficiency/Practical Test: FAR 61.103(f), 61.107(b), 61.109

IACRA vs. Paper Application

The instructor and student must complete the IACRA rating application online at iacra.faa.gov, or complete and sign Form 8710-1 for the examiner at the practical test. Most examiners now prefer IACRA.

Medical Requirements

Except in certain instances, the applicant must hold at least a current third-class medical certificate (FAR 61.23(a)(3)(iii)).

ZZPGM|gs:additional-ratings|ZZ

5. Additional Ratings & Retesting

Additional Class Rating — FAR 61.63(c)

For an additional class rating (e.g., adding multiengine to a single-engine private pilot certificate), the applicant needs:

  • AC 61-65 A.78 – Additional Aircraft Category or Class Rating (other than ATP): FAR 61.63(c)
  • AC 61-65 A.1 – Practical test endorsement
  • Other endorsements as required (e.g., A.72 for complex aircraft if applicable)

No knowledge test is required provided the applicant already holds a rating at the same certificate level. No need to meet the time requirements applicable to the initial class rating.

Additional Category Rating — FAR 61.63(b)

Complete all applicable aeronautical experience and training, then receive endorsements A.78 + A.1 (plus others as required) and pass the practical test.

Example: Single-Engine Private Pilot Adding Multiengine Rating

  1. AC 61-65 A.1 – Prerequisite for a Practical Test: FAR 61.39(a)(6)(i)&(ii)
  2. AC 61-65 A.78 – Additional Aircraft Category or Class Rating (other than ATP): FAR 61.63(c)
  3. AC 61-65 A.72 – To act as PIC in a complex aircraft: FAR 61.31(e) (if applicable)

Solo Flight Without Appropriate Category/Class — FAR 61.31(d)(2)

If a pilot does not hold the appropriate category/class rating, they must have received the required training. Endorsement: AC 61-65 A.76 – Solo PIC when the pilot does not hold the appropriate category/class.

Retesting After Disapproval — FAR 61.43(f) & 61.49

  • A practical test, whether satisfactory or not, uses up the endorsement for that test
  • The applicant must receive additional instruction and a new endorsement before retesting: AC 61-65 A.77 – Retesting after failure of a knowledge or practical test: FAR 61.49
  • An instructor recommendation (IACRA or 8710) is required for every retest
  • The applicant may receive credit for Areas of Operation already passed if the remainder is completed within 60 calendar days after discontinuation

After a Letter of Discontinuance

  • No additional endorsements required
  • Credit is given for areas already passed if the test is completed within 60 calendar days
  • After 60 calendar days, the entire practical test must be re-accomplished
ZZPGM|gs:time-limits|ZZ

6. Time Limits: 60 Calendar Days vs. 2 Calendar Months

60 Calendar-Day Limit — FAR 61.43(e)-(f)

A practical test may be discontinued for four reasons:

  1. Failing one or more areas of operation
  2. Inclement weather
  3. Airworthiness concerns
  4. Safety of flight concern

If discontinued, the applicant receives credit for areas already passed. The remainder of the test must be completed within 60 calendar days (FAR 61.43(f)(1)). After 60 calendar days, all areas must be re-tested from the beginning.

2 Calendar-Month Limit — FAR 61.39(g)-(h)

If all increments of a practical test are not completed on the same date — whether due to discontinuance or because the test was planned in increments — all remaining increments must be completed within 2 calendar months (FAR 61.39(g)). After 2 calendar months, the entire test must be re-accomplished (FAR 61.39(h)).

Key Distinction

These two time limits are separate. The 60-day limit governs credit for passed areas after discontinuance; the 2-calendar-month limit governs completion of a test conducted in planned increments. Neither is related to the 90-day endorsement window for student solo flights.

ZZPGM|gs:flight-review|ZZ

7. Flight Review & Instrument Proficiency Check Endorsements

Flight Review Completion — AC 61-65 A.69

After satisfactory completion of a flight review, the instructor must endorse the pilot's logbook per FAR 61.56(a)&(c). No entry reflecting unsatisfactory performance is required, but instruction given should be recorded.

Instrument Proficiency Check (IPC) — AC 61-65 A.71

A CFII is required to conduct an IPC for instrument-rated pilots. After satisfactory completion, endorse the pilot's logbook per FAR 61.57(d). As with the flight review, no unsatisfactory-performance entry is required, but log the instruction given.

ZZPGM|gs:instructor-responsibilities|ZZ

8. Flight Instructor Responsibilities

Recordkeeping — FAR 61.189

An instructor must maintain a logbook or separate document containing:

  • Name of each person endorsed for solo flight privileges, and the date of the endorsement
  • Name of each person endorsed for a knowledge or practical test, with the kind of test, date, and results

Records must be retained for at least 3 years.

Limitations & Expiration Dates

Failure to ensure proper endorsements is a serious performance deficiency. Depending on the situation, the FAA could hold the instructor accountable. Required limitations and expiration dates exist for safety — ensure proper endorsements and confirm the learner understands them.

Training Initial Flight Instructor Applicants (Effective December 1, 2024)

Ground training options — the trainer must have:

  • Held the appropriate instructor certificate for 24+ months and given 40+ hours of ground training, OR
  • Held the appropriate instructor certificate and given 100+ hours of ground training in an FAA-approved course

Flight training options — the trainer must have:

  • Held a flight instructor certificate for at least 24 months and given at least 200 hours of flight training, OR
  • Maintained an 80% practical test pass rate for at least 5 applicants in the last 24 months, OR
  • Provided 200 hours of flight training and completed a Flight Instructor Enhanced Qualification Training Program (FIEQTP) under Part 141 — per FAR 61.95(h)(3) and AC 61-145
ZZPGM|gs:cfi-certificate|ZZ

9. Maintaining Your CFI Certificate & WINGS Program

Duration of Certificates (Effective December 1, 2024)

  • Certificates issued before December 1, 2024 expire 24 calendar months from the month issued, renewed, or reinstated (Exception: FAR 61.197(b))
  • Certificates issued on or after December 1, 2024 are issued without an expiration date

Recent Experience Requirements — FAR 61.197

Within the previous 24 calendar months, satisfy one of the following:

  1. Pass a practical test for one of the ratings listed on the instructor certificate, or for an additional flight instructor rating
  2. Submit documentation showing endorsement of 5+ applicants for a checkride with an 80%+ first-attempt pass rate (a Gold Seal certificate may be applied for/renewed at the same time)
  3. Serve as a company check pilot or check airman, chief flight instructor, Part 121 or 135 instructor, or similar evaluative position within the past 24 calendar months
  4. Complete an approved flight instructor refresher course within the past 3 calendar months (see AC 61-83)
  5. Pass a military instructor pilot or pilot examiner proficiency check in an aircraft within the past 24 calendar months
  6. Complete an FAA-sponsored pilot proficiency program (WINGS) — see requirements below

WINGS Program Requirements — AC 61-91

  • Hold a current flight instructor certificate
  • Complete at least 1 phase of an FAA-sponsored pilot proficiency program in the last 12 months
  • Evaluate and endorse 15 flight activities (at least 5 pilots) under the pilot proficiency program

Reinstatement of Flight Instructor Privileges — FAR 61.199 (Effective December 1, 2024)

If a certificate has expired:

  • Within 3 calendar months of expiration: Privileges can be reinstated via an approved FIRC (Flight Instructor Refresher Course). No instructional privileges during this reinstatement period.
  • After 3 calendar months: Must pass an instructor practical test for one of the ratings on the expired certificate, a practical test for an additional flight instructor rating, or a military instructor pilot/pilot examiner proficiency check

Documentation

Submit an Airman Certificate and/or Rating Application (Form 8710-1 or 8710-11) to validate recent experience.

ZZPGM|gs:conclusion|ZZ

10. Conclusion & Verification

Understanding logbook requirements and endorsement procedures is essential for every flight instructor. Proper records protect both student and instructor — ensuring training is documented, certificates remain valid, and the FAA's requirements are met.

Before endorsing a student or recommending an applicant for a practical test, verify that all required training has been completed, appropriate time limits are satisfied, and endorsement language matches current AC 61-65K model text.

Important Reminder

This site is a reference aid. Always verify endorsement applicability against the pilot's specific context, current FARs, and current FAA guidance — including the latest edition of AC 61-65.

Official References

  • AC 61-65K – Certification: Pilots and Flight and Ground Instructors
  • AC 61-98 – Currency Requirements and Guidance for the Flight Review and IPC
  • AC 61-83 – Flight Instructor Refresher Course
  • AC 61-91 – WINGS Pilot Proficiency Program
  • FAA Order 8900.1 (FSIMS)
